conceptTag: Find the moat in a local bakery
readerTitle: Your croissant is not your moat
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 베이커리의 소매·카페 납품, 베이커리용 주문 소프트웨어) · 모든 인물과 수치는 설명용
insight: 좋은 제품은 해자가 아니다. 경쟁자가 똑같은 제품을 내일 내놓아도 고객이 남는 이유가 해자다.
misconception: 동네에서 제일 맛있는 빵을 만들면 그 자체로 경쟁에서 지켜진다.

sources.text: 모든 인물, 업체, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시
전환 비용과 규모의 경제(배송 밀도)는 경쟁 전략의 표준 개념

factChecks.note: 모든 수치(카페 40곳, 반경 3km, 25km 거리, 10% 할인, 베이커리 300곳)는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 실제 통계로 읽히지 않는지 문구를 확인하세요.
배송 밀도를 '지역 단위 규모의 경제'로 설명했습니다. STR-04-02의 정의 및 용어와 표현이 일치하는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Your croissant is not your moat
body: Marta runs a bakery with a small shop and a bigger business behind it. Every morning at 5 a.m., her van delivers pastries to 40 cafés nearby.
Then a national bakery chain opens two blocks away. Her regulars swear her croissants are better. That feels like protection. It probably isn't the protection that matters.

image.label: A small bakery van leaving at dawn while a chain store opens nearby
image.brief: 새벽 거리. 작은 동네 베이커리 앞에서 배달 밴이 출발하고, 두 블록 떨어진 곳에 커다란 체인 베이커리 간판이 막 불을 켬. 따뜻한 색감. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What protects Marta most?
body: The chain can copy her croissant and match her price within a few months. Which of these would still keep her business?

options.text: Her croissants really are the best in town
options.feedback: A better product wins today, but recipes can be copied. A moat is what still works once a rival makes the same thing at the same price.

options.text: The 40 cafés whose menus and morning routines are built around her deliveries
options.feedback: This is a **switching cost**. Leaving her means risk and effort for each café, even if a rival's pastry is just as good.

options.text: Everyone in the neighborhood knows her name
options.feedback: Local fame helps. It only counts as a **brand** moat if it makes people pay more or keep coming when the chain is cheaper.

cards.title: Ask what survives a perfect copy.
body: Imagine the chain makes Marta's exact croissant tomorrow at her exact price. What still brings customers back to her?
Not the recipe. That was the thing being copied. So look at what sits *around* the product: who depends on her, how she delivers, and what customers would lose by leaving.
Marta has three candidates. They are not equally strong.

cards.title: Three possible moats, three strengths.
body: Only one candidate is strong today. One more could become strong if she builds it on purpose.

breakdown.label: Dense delivery route
breakdown.detail: 40 cafés within 3 km keeps cost per drop low

breakdown.label: Café accounts
breakdown.detail: Menus, timing and trust built around her

cards.title: Why a café owner won't switch for 10% off.
body: The chain offers cafés a 10% discount. Most say no.

For a café, switching is not just a new price. It means reprinting menus, retraining staff on new bake times, and trusting a stranger to show up at 5 a.m. One missed Monday means an empty pastry case at the morning rush.
That risk is the **switching cost**. It's Marta's moat. But it lives in her customers' heads, so it only lasts while her deliveries stay boringly reliable.

image.label: A café counter with a full pastry case and a delivery schedule on the wall
image.brief: 카페 카운터 뒤편. 꽉 찬 페이스트리 진열장, 벽에 붙은 '5:00 delivery' 일정표, 직원 교육용 굽기 시간표. 반대편에 비어 있는 진열장을 흐리게 넣어 '바꿨을 때의 위험'을 암시. 로고 없음.

cards.title: A new account, 25 km away.
body: A hotel 25 km outside town wants daily pastries. It would be Marta's biggest single account. All her other stops sit within 3 km, so the van finishes before 7 a.m.

options.text: Take it. More volume is always good
options.feedback: She gains revenue but spreads her route thin. Her **scale** edge is density: many drops close together. One far stop raises her cost per delivery and can delay everyone else.

options.text: Pass for now and chase more cafés inside her 3 km zone
options.feedback: This protects **local scale**. Each nearby stop lowers her cost per delivery, and a distant rival can't match that cost on her streets.

options.text: Take it, but add a delivery fee
options.feedback: The fee covers fuel, not the risk of late deliveries to her core cafés. It could work if the hotel order runs on a separate trip.

cards.title: A moat you don't maintain quietly drains.
body: Switching costs protect Marta only while switching feels risky. If her deliveries turn late or sloppy, that same café owner starts to see switching as the *safer* choice.
Route density works the same way. If the chain builds its own dense route nearby, her cost edge shrinks.
Name the moat, then spend effort keeping it. Don't assume it will stay.

cards.title: Now it's an ordering app for bakeries.
body: A small company sells online ordering software to 300 independent bakeries. Their café customers place standing orders through it. A large rival launches a free version with more features.
What is most likely to keep the bakeries?

options.text: Shipping more features than the rival
options.feedback: Features are the croissant recipe of software. The rival can copy them, and it has more engineers.

options.text: The cafés' standing orders, price lists and order history already live in the app
options.feedback: Two layers of **switching costs**: the bakery must move its data, and every café must change its habits. Free doesn't erase that work.

options.text: Being the name bakers recommend to each other
options.feedback: Word of mouth helps win new users. It protects against "free" only if bakers trust it enough to stay.

cards.title: Look past the product to find the moat.
body: Today you used **switching costs** (cafés that rely on Marta's mornings, users whose data lives in the app), **scale** as route density, and the **brand** test: does the name change what customers pay or do?
**Try it today:** imagine a rival copies your best product tomorrow at your price. Write down the one reason customers would stay. If you can't name one, that's your project.
